payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a dispatch that ran without usage capture when its run record is written then the recorded command carries no usage-report flag and a test asserts the recorded command matches the real argv with only the prompt redacted
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "REDACTED_PROMPT, capture_usage=True" src/basicly/runner.py
uv run python -c "
import json, pathlib
recs=[json.loads(l) for l in pathlib.Path('.basicly/usage/records.jsonl').read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()]
print([r.get('command') for r in recs if r.get('phase')=='decide'][:2])"
```

Observed - a `phase: decide` record's `command` ends in the usage-report flags, but `decisions.py:655` dispatches with `capture_usage` unset, so those flags were never on the real argv. Expected - the recorded command is the command that ran, modulo the redacted prompt.

## Context

`runner.record_dispatch` (runner.py:1593-1596) re-derives the command instead of copying `result.command`, and it must: the real argv embeds the prompt, and the record stores `REDACTED_PROMPT` in its place. The defect is that it hard-codes `capture_usage=True` in that re-derivation rather than threading through the flag the dispatch actually used.

So every dispatch that ran without usage capture records a command asserting it did. That is the `ipx2` class - a claim committed beside the thing it is wrong about - and it lands in the one artifact a later session uses to reconstruct what happened. It cost time on `basicly-gczc`: the record is what you read to ask whether a dispatch captured usage, and it answers yes for a dispatch that did not.

Found 2026-08-03 while mapping stdout consumers for gczc's fix.

**Note the masking, because it is the reason to fix this now rather than later.** `gczc` makes `decisions.py` and `rubrics.py` pass `capture_usage=True`, and `loop.py`/`supervise.py` already do - so once gczc lands there is no call site left whose record diverges, and the defect becomes invisible while remaining armed for the next call site that records without capture. Thread the flag; do not rely on every future caller passing True.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
payload.title: The recorded dispatch command claims usage flags the real argv never carried

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a completed code lane whose actual spend is recorded when its forecast is compared against that actual then the ratio is within one order of magnitude and a test fails when recorded evidence puts it outside that bound
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
import json, pathlib
r = json.loads(pathlib.Path('.basicly/usage/run-records.json').read_text())['basicly-gczc'][0]
print({k: r.get(k) for k in ('forecast_tokens','forecast_source','scope_tokens','context_tokens','tokens','cost','duration_s','task_class')})"
```

Observed - measured on the 2026-08-03 `basicly-gczc` lane, a single-track `loop run` on a bug with an eight-file declared scope:

| field | value |
| --- | --- |
| `forecast_tokens` | 66780 |
| `forecast_source` | dispatch |
| `scope_tokens` | 32000 |
| `context_tokens` | 210721 |
| `tokens` (actual, adapter-measured) | **16963245** |
| `cost` | 12.03 |
| `duration_s` | 1342 |

**actual / forecast = 254x.** Expected - a forecast that admits a pass against a grant is within an order of magnitude of what the pass spends.

## Context

This is the defect `u6jq.1` is blocked on, and it is **not fixed**. The plan's diagnosis of the failed 2026-07-26 proof run was that D8 forecasts *working set*, under-forecasts it 2.8-4.8x, and does not model turn count at all, while an agentic loop re-sends its context every turn - so spend came out 160-420x the forecast. 254x sits inside that band. Every bead in the forecast chain is closed (`jr0l.21` per-model calibration, `jr0l.22` pass admission, `jr0l.34` forecast/actual pairing, `jr0l.35` estimate metering, `vz78`, `jr0l.16` band-at-dispatch, plus `fcls`, `z2wi` and `3w44` on the sizing side), and the error is the same order it was before them.

What the chain did fix is real and should not be re-litigated: the numbers are now *recorded* (this bead exists because `jr0l.34` paired them and `fcls` added `context_tokens`), and the sizer no longer refuses everything. What it did not fix is the forecast's *unit*: 66780 is a working-set figure and 16963245 is a whole-lane spend, so the two are denominated in different quantities - the exact `z2wi` shape, one level up from the build factor.

Two facts in the same record show where the missing term is. `context_tokens` 210721 is 6.6x `scope_tokens` 32000, so even the ambient context is far larger than the scope model predicts; and 16963245 / 210721 = 80, which is the turn multiplier nothing models.

**Consequence for the release.** A grant sized from a forecast is sized wrong: this lane was dispatched under an 8000000-token L3 grant and spent 16963245, so the grant halted after the work was done and the ship checkpoint dropped to a human. The engine behaved correctly at every step - it is the number that was wrong.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/run_record.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
- `tests/test_run_record.py`
payload.title: The dispatch forecast under-predicts a real code lane by two orders of magnitude

payload.text:
Blocked on basicly-tcmy.5, decided 2026-08-03 while composing the wave-two pass. Two reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one.

Mechanically, tcmy.34's declared scope is a strict subset of tcmy.5's - decompose.py, run_record.py and both their test files - and both change the same forecast functions, so as concurrent lanes they collide in the merge queue rather than in a region a rebase can resolve.

Substantively, tcmy.34 must calibrate a whole-lane multiplier over the recorded population, and tcmy.5 is what makes that population correct: unsized_lane_tokens reads only phase=='lane' so 113 build records are invisible to it, and calibrated_build_factors filters on no phase at all so decider and rubric dispatches are eligible samples. Fitting a multiplier before that lands is fitting to a filtered population - the basicly-ipx2 mistake, where a filter on an optional field silently selected a sub-population and the conclusion was committed as a rationale.

Note for whoever picks tcmy.34 up: its first action is a measurement, not a code change. Compute the actual/forecast distribution across every run record carrying both fields before choosing any model, and if the paired sample is too small to fit, write needs-input rather than inventing a factor. One sample (16963245/66780 = 254x) is an existence proof, not a calibration.

The population measurement is done, 2026-08-03, and it narrows this bead substantially. Two findings.

**1. 254x was the median, not an outlier.** Across every run record carrying both a forecast and an adapter-measured actual (n=14): median **269x**, range 1x to 591x, spread 466x. So the under-prediction is systematic rather than a property of one lane. Worst cases: vkh0.10 at 591x (26780 forecast, 15830484 actual), tcmy.10 at 533x, tcmy.8 at 519x. 19 further records carry tokens but no forecast at all, so they cannot be paired.

**2. The engine already computes a realistic whole-lane figure - it just does not record it.** The wave-two pass admission on 2026-08-03 forecast **55937094 tokens for three sized lanes (18645698 per lane)** and refused the pass against a 55000000 grant. That figure is the right order of magnitude: the three comparable measured lanes came in at 16963245 (gczc), 15830484 (vkh0.10) and 10673516 (jr0l.64). Meanwhile each of those records' own `forecast_tokens` field held a working-set number in the tens of thousands.

So there are **two estimators roughly 280x apart**: `admit_pass_spend` produces a whole-lane spend forecast that binds a gate correctly, and `record_dispatch` writes a working-set figure into the field named `forecast_tokens`, which `jr0l.34`'s forecast/actual pairing then compares against a whole-lane actual. That comparison is the unit mismatch, and it is the same z2wi shape one level up.

**Consequence for the fix.** Do not build a new calibration first. Establish which quantity each estimator reports, then make the recorded field the one the admission gate already trusts - or record both and name them distinctly. A calibration fitted to the current field would be fitting a correction factor to a units error, which is how z2wi's build factor reached 216.65 against a seed of 3.0.

The spread still matters after that: 466x across 14 records means even the correct-unit forecast will need a per-class factor rather than one constant, and `context_tokens` (recorded since fcls) is the term to correlate against - the three records that carry it show actual/context of 82x, 82x and 63x, far tighter than actual/forecast.

Sequencing fact measured 2026-08-05 at d31f6bd, and it adds a prerequisite this bead did not have.

  uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-yc0x
  spend cal: SEEDS - no model pinned, so no sample can key in; paired write
             dispatches: bug 0/10, chore 0/10, task 0/10
  factors:   all seeds (never measured) - bug 2, chore 1.5, task 3

So the calibration population is not merely small, it is structurally **empty**: every factor is still the seeded value, and 0 of 10 paired write dispatches have keyed in for any of the three task classes. The reason preflight gives is basicly-tcmy.35 - this repo declares no model tier, so a dispatch records no model and a per-model calibration sample has no key to land under.

That splits this bead's work cleanly along a line worth respecting:

- **The unit fix does not depend on tcmy.35.** Establishing that admit_pass_spend reports whole-lane spend while record_dispatch writes a working-set figure into forecast_tokens, and making the recorded field the one the admission gate already trusts, is pure code and can be done now. This is the half the bead is titled for and the half u6jq.1 is blocked on.
- **Any calibration half is blocked until a tier is declared.** Fitting a per-class factor while 0 of 10 samples can key in would fit to the seeds - which is the basicly-ipx2 shape again, a filter (here, a missing key) silently selecting an empty sub-population, and worse than the z2wi units error because an empty fit looks like a converged one.

Recommendation: land the unit fix under this bead and do not touch the factors. tcmy.35 was placed in v0.9.0 by the plan's ladder; on this evidence it belongs in v0.7.0, because until it lands no forecast number this repo records can be calibrated against anything - including the numbers u6jq.1 exists to measure.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a metered dispatch in this repo when it runs then a declared tier resolved its model and the record names the tier and whether it was honoured or a check refuses the dispatch
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "default_tier|\[\[runner.agents\]\]" basicly.toml basicly.local.toml
uv run python -c "
import json, pathlib
r = json.loads(pathlib.Path('.basicly/usage/run-records.json').read_text())['basicly-gczc'][0]
print({k: r.get(k) for k in ('model','model_tier','model_source','tier_honoured','model_mismatch','observed_models')})"
```

Observed - on the 2026-08-03 `basicly-gczc` lane: `model`, `model_tier`, `model_source`, `tier_honoured` and `model_mismatch` are all `None`, while `observed_models` is `['claude-haiku-4-5', 'claude-opus-5']` - two different models served one dispatch. No `[runner] default_tier` and no `[[runner.agents]]` entry exists in `basicly.toml` or the local overlay. Expected - the repo that ships the tier vocabulary declares one.

## Context

The resolver is built and correct: `kjc5.58` established the tier vocabulary, `kjc5.61` generates the committed map, `kjc5.59` refuses an unresolved tier before spawning anything, and `models.py:69` raises when a tier was declared and no model could be pinned. Note the precondition - **a tier was declared**. Nothing in this repo declares one, so the refusal is unreachable and every dispatch runs on whatever the agent CLI defaulted to that day.

That is the Phase S shape one level up from the usual: the instrument is wired to the engine, and nothing supplies the input that makes it act. It is also invisible to every existing gate, because an absent tier is indistinguishable from a deliberate no-tier choice.

**Why it matters now rather than at Phase 1.** `7bur` measures cost per landed package and the plan already records the constraint: measuring tier economics against an unpinned mapping produces a number about nothing. `u6jq.1`'s proof run has the same exposure - it would report a cost for an unnamed model. And the same record shows the cost is real: this dispatch spent 16963245 tokens for 12.03 dollars with no record of what ran it.

Fix is a config declaration plus a gate, not engine work: declare `[runner] default_tier`, then make an absent tier on a metered dispatch fail a check rather than pass silently. `basicly-a3yi` is the adjacent projection half.

## Scope

- `basicly.toml`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `tests/test_config.py`

## Context

The four residual findings from the 2026-08-03 review of `basicly-gczc`, none blocking, grouped because they are all one theme: the judge half of that fix is asserted more weakly than the decider half, and three small claims are wider than what a test pins.

1. **The judge has no meter-level proof.** `tests/test_decisions.py` asserts `policy.spend_status(...).halted is False` over records the real `record_dispatch` wrote, plus a control that fails without the fix. The judge side asserts `seen['capture_usage'] is True` and stubs `record_dispatch` out entirely in its unwrap test. Per the rule the bead itself invoked - a passing parser is not evidence about a fail-open gate - the judge deserves the same assertion, and it matters more, because `rubrics.evaluate` runs on **every** validated lane while the decider runs only on a delegated decision.

2. **`basicly runner dry-run` prints an argv a real dispatch would not send.** `cli.py:3525` does not pass `capture_usage`, so the printed command omits the usage flags a metered dispatch appends. Harmless to metering, but `runner.py:226` claims every command is printable via `runner dry-run`, and this one is printable as something else.

## The failure this comes from

I ran `git checkout HEAD -- tests/test_cli.py` during basicly-vkh0.42 and lost two of my
own uncommitted edits. Nothing refused it. The `require-explicit-confirmation` fragment
names the family in as many words, and the permissions comment
(`.basicly/core/permissions/permissions.yaml:34`) names these three commands *specifically*
as undenied — so the rule was written, read and still not followed.

**Root cause: the rule lives only in prose, and prose is advisory at the moment of the
call.** Every neighbouring family in that file has a mechanical backstop —
`destructive-rm`, `destructive-git`, `bypass-gates`, `force-push`. This one has a comment
explaining why it does not. The asymmetry is what made it the family that got through.

## The control

A `destructive-restore` deny entry beside `destructive-git`:

## The failure this comes from

A multi-line regex I ran over `tests/test_decompose.py` during basicly-vkh0.42 removed
**1644 lines**. The pattern was `(?:    .*\n)+?(?=\n\n)`, intended to cut one indented
block; the lazy quantifier still spanned every blank-line-separated run in the file. The
module was restored from HEAD and every edit reapplied by hand.

## Why the existing rule did not catch it

The `non-interactive-shell` fragment already says to name the expected site count before a
scripted multi-site replace and reconcile after. It did not bind here, for two reasons:

- **A deletion's site count was right.** One match, as predicted. The match was the wrong
  *size*, and a count of matches cannot see size.
- The rule reads as being about replacement, so an edit framed as a cut does not obviously
  fall under it.

## The control

Extend that fragment with the magnitude clause: after any scripted in-place edit, compare
`wc -l` before and against after, and name the expected delta first. A delta larger than
the change described is a stop, the same way a site-count delta is. One line, in the
fragment that already carries the site-count rule, so it lands in every agent's always-on
baseline — check the character budget before adding, since that baseline is at its cap.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the `non-interactive-shell` fragment when it is read then it names the line-delta
  reconciliation for a scripted in-place edit, distinct from the site-count rule
- Given the projected instruction files when `basicly check` runs then every per-target
  character cap still passes

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/non-interactive-shell.yaml`

payload.description:
## The defect

The repository declares one toolchain floor, `requires-python = ">=3.14"`, and pins nothing else. Continuous integration floats `uv` to latest and pins node to an older major than this machine runs, so a gate can pass locally and fail in continuous integration, or the reverse, and no measurement would say which.

Measured 2026-08-19.

| tool | this machine | continuous integration | direction of skew |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| uv | 0.11.28 | unpinned, `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` resolves latest, which is 0.12.5 released 2026-08-14 | local **behind** |
| node | 24.18.0 | `node-version: 22` in two workflows | local **ahead** by two majors |
| git | 2.43.0, and the distribution candidate is also 2.43.0 | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, whatever that image ships | local behind, by an unmeasured amount |
| python | 3.14.6 | resolved by uv from `requires-python` | local behind 3.14.7, released 2026-08-05 |

## Why this is a defect rather than housekeeping

A behaviour difference between the two is already demonstrable. `uv init` gained a default build system in uv 0.12.0, released 2026-08-28... corrected: released 2026-07-28. So the same command produces a different project layout on this machine than in continuous integration, today. `uv init --help` on 0.11.28 lists both `--package` and `--no-package`, so a flag probe does not reveal it and only running the command does.

The repository is a distribution installed into other repositories, so its own gates are the product. A gate whose outcome depends on an unpinned tool version is a gate whose outcome nobody can reproduce.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `uv --version` locally and read 0.11.28.
2. Read `.github/workflows/quality-gates.yml` and `basicly.yml` and observe `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` with no version input.
3. Fetch the current uv release and observe 0.12.5.
4. Read `node-version: 22` in both workflows and compare with `node --version` locally, 24.18.0.
5. Observe that no file in the tree states a version for uv, node or git.

Observed: three tools skew in two directions and nothing declares an expected version.
Expected: the toolchain a gate runs on is declared, and a difference is visible rather than latent.

## The decision this needs, recorded rather than assumed

Whether to pin continuous integration to the local toolchain, or to raise the local toolchain to what continuous integration resolves, or to declare a floor and a ceiling per tool and check both. This record does not choose. What it refuses is the current state, where neither side is declared.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the repository when a reader asks what toolchain a gate expects then a declared version or range answers, per tool, for uv and node and git.
- Given continuous integration when it provisions a tool then it provisions the declared version rather than resolving latest.
- Given a local toolchain outside the declared range when a gate runs then it says so rather than passing silently.
- Given a declared range when a tool releases a new version then nothing fails until a human widens the range.
- Demonstrated by: a check that reads the declared toolchain and the running one and fails on a mismatch, run once with a deliberately wrong local version and once green

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `.scripts/`
- `tests/`

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
import json, pathlib
from collections import Counter
recs = [json.loads(l) for l in pathlib.Path('.basicly/usage/records.jsonl').read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()]
print(Counter(r.get('phase') for r in recs))
"
rg -n "phase=\"build\"" src/basicly/loop.py
rg -n "phase=\"lane\"" src/basicly/supervise.py
rg -n 'phase.*==.*"lane"' src/basicly/decompose.py
```

Observed - the same kind of write dispatch is recorded under two phase names (`build` and `lane`); `unsized_lane_tokens` counts only `lane`, and `calibrated_build_factors` filters on no phase at all so decider and rubric dispatches are eligible samples. Expected - one named set of write phases read by both.

## Context

The same work is recorded under two phase names: `loop._run_agent` records a build dispatch as `phase='build'` (loop.py:627) and `supervise._dispatch_lane` records the same kind of work as `phase='lane'` (supervise.py:2178). Measured across 184 beads: `{'build': 113, 'lane': 17, 'probe': 1, None: 61}`.

Two consumers filter oppositely. `decompose.unsized_lane_tokens` (decompose.py:1142) requires `phase == 'lane'`, so all 113 build records are invisible to the ceiling that bounds an unsizeable lane - even though the interactive path is the documented default on this machine. `decompose.calibrated_build_factors` (decompose.py:678) filters on no phase at all, so decider and rubric dispatches are eligible build-factor samples.

Related and in the same seam: `calibrated_build_factors` has never calibrated. Nine qualifying samples against `calibration_min_samples = 10` per class, so it returns `DEFAULT_BUILD_FACTOR_SEEDS` unchanged. `SpendForecast` carries a calibration marker and `unsized_lane_tokens` returns a `measured`/`seed` source precisely so a seed cannot be mistaken for a measurement, but `CostEstimate.build_factor` is a bare float and `record_inputs()` does not record where it came from.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a write dispatch recorded from either the interactive or the supervised path when the unsizeable-lane bound is computed then both are counted, because one named constant defines the write phases
- Given the build-factor calibration when it samples run records then decider and rubric dispatches are excluded
- Given an estimate whose build factor came from the seed when the dispatch is recorded then the record states that it was seeded rather than measured
- Given the per-class sample counts when loop preflight runs then it reports whether calibration is still on seeds

## Scope

- `src/basicly/run_record.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `tests/test_run_record.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/rubrics.py`
- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `tests/test_cli_loop.py`
- `tests/test_config.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "gate_from_unreliable_escalation" src/ tests/
rg -n "_carry_out_rework_retry" -A 12 src/basicly/cli.py
```

Observed - `gate_from_unreliable_escalation` has references only in tests; the one place an escalation answer is carried out calls `policy.gate_from_rework_escalation`, whose regex does not match the unreliable question, so it returns None and bails. Answering 'land anyway' therefore only releases the lane, the landing re-attempts, the flaky gate trips again and the identical item is re-enqueued under the next generation. Expected - the offered remedy is carried out, or it is not offered.

## Context

`loop._unreliable_landing_block` (loop.py:826) enqueues, at MAX_UNRELIABLE_GATE_EVENTS, the question 'gate <g> is unreliable: it failed and then passed unchanged 3 times; fix the flake, or land anyway?'. `policy.gate_from_unreliable_escalation` (policy.py:560) was written to parse that question back and has zero production call sites - only tests.

The one place an escalation answer is carried out, `cli._carry_out_rework_retry` (cli.py:3354), matches `^\s*retry\b` then calls `policy.gate_from_rework_escalation`, whose regex only matches the rework question and returns None here. So answering 'land anyway' merely releases the lane, the landing re-attempts, the same flaky gate trips, the counter passes the bound again and `decisions.enqueue` re-opens the item under the next generation - an unbounded ladder of identical questions with the offered remedy unimplemented.

This is basicly-4tjt verbatim, quoted at policy.py:467: the escalation offered three choices and implemented none of them. Same shape, one incident later, in the sibling escalation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an unreliable-gate escalation answered land anyway when the lane is next processed then the landing proceeds once under an explicit override rather than re-running the same gate
- Given the same escalation answered any way at all when the lane is processed then the identical question is not re-enqueued under a new generation
- Given the escalation question text when the engine parses an answer then the parser used has a production call site

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli_policy.py`

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "Ship does not merge|Ship merges to the entry branch" .basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml
rg -n "not on a bare .policy checkpoint|policy checkpoint <id> classify" .basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml
rg -n "def _on_ship" -A 15 src/basicly/loop.py
```

Observed - the skill says both 'Ship does not merge and does not publish' and 'Ship merges to the entry branch recorded at intake'; `_on_ship` tears down and closes and never merges. Separately the skill warns not to relay a confirm code onto a bare `policy checkpoint --approve` and then its phases table prescribes exactly that. Expected - no statement in the skill contradicts another or the code.

## Context

Two self-contradictions in one skill source, both on the paths that cost this repo real incidents.

1. Ship. Line 122 states 'Ship does not merge and does not publish - the merge already happened at the build->verify landing, and ship naming it otherwise is what caused the recorded mis-approval (basicly-jr0l.39)'. Line 273 states 'Ship merges to the entry branch recorded at intake (default: main), tears down the worktree, and closes the issue'. The code (loop.py:380 `_on_ship`) tears down, closes and refuses an unmerged branch; it never merges. The wrong half is verbatim the wording jr0l.39 exists about.

2. Checkpoints. Line 104 warns to relay a confirm code on the printed `loop run` command and 'not on a bare policy checkpoint --approve, or the checkpoint is approved and the loop stays parked'. Line 156's phases table then gives exactly `basicly policy checkpoint <id> classify --approve` as the way to advance. Because `policy._confirm_key` (policy.py:610) keys the code by issue and checkpoint rather than by command, relaying it onto the bare form succeeds and silently produces the parked state.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the harness-loop skill when it describes the ship phase then every mention says ship tears down and closes and none says it merges
- Given the phases table when it names how to pass a checkpoint then it names the loop run form and marks policy checkpoint as inspection-only
- Given the projected skill after the change when the projection gates run then they are green

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the release-process guidance when the catalog is built then it projects from a skill.yaml source and a hand-authored SKILL.md under a projected root is reported by the projection gates rather than passing silently
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
ls .basicly/core/skills/release-process        # No such file or directory
ls .claude/skills/release-process/SKILL.md      # exists, tracked, no generated marker
ls .agents/skills/release-process               # absent, so Codex never sees it
uv run basicly skills-check --all-default-roots # exits 0
```

Observed - a hand-authored SKILL.md lives in a projected output directory with no catalog source, and every projection gate reports green. Expected - the skill projects from a `skill.yaml` source, and a hand-authored file under a projected root is reported rather than ignored.

## Context

`.claude/skills/release-process/SKILL.md` is tracked, hand-written, carries no generated marker, and has no `.basicly/core/skills/release-process/skill.yaml`. It is therefore absent from `.agents/skills/` so Codex never sees it, and invisible to every gate: `basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` exits 0, `catalog lint` only scans under `.basicly/core/`, and the projection manifest holds 5 outputs so protect-generated-commit does not cover skills either.

For a product whose core claim is one catalog projected into agent files with drift gates, a skill the projector does not know about is a hole in the value proposition.

The content is also self-contradictory: line 10 says 'Use basicly release - do not hand-run the preparation steps' and line 32 explains that curating afterwards is the trap it replaced, then lines 81-116 give a full hand-run workflow whose commit subject ('docs(release): update changelog for <release>') would fail this repo's own commit-msg hook, and which pushes before tagging. It also documents `### Highlights` and `### Commit delta` sections that CHANGELOG.md does not contain.

A stray hand-written `.claude/skills/README.md` reinforces the wrong model and should go with it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the release-process guidance when the catalog is built then it is projected from a skill.yaml source under .basicly/core/skills like every other skill
- Given a hand-authored SKILL.md placed under a projected skills root when the projection gates run then they report it rather than exiting zero
- Given the surviving release-process content when it is read then it describes only basicly release plus the two steps that command does not do

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/release-process/skill.yaml`
- `.claude/skills/release-process/**`
- `.claude/skills/README.md`
- `src/basicly/skills.py`

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "^WORK_TYPES" src/basicly/config.py
rg -n "canonical enum" .basicly/core/skills/tool-br/skill.yaml
uv run basicly worktree --help | head -3
rg -n "not yet part of" .basicly/core/skills/worktree-isolation/skill.yaml
rg -n "DEFAULT_WORKTREE_CONCURRENCY" src/basicly/config.py
rg -n "default 4" .basicly/core/skills/worktree-isolation/skill.yaml
```

Observed - the skill advertises `docs` and `question` work types that `WORK_TYPES` excludes and `classify` raises on; it says worktree merging is 'not yet part of basicly worktree' while `merge` and `merge-queue` are shipped subcommands; and it documents a concurrency default of 4 against `DEFAULT_WORKTREE_CONCURRENCY = 5`. Expected - each claim matches the code.

## Context

Three stale claims an agent would act on.

1. `tool-br/skill.yaml:203` says the type taxonomy is br's canonical enum including `docs` and `question`. `config.py:453` defines `WORK_TYPES = ('bug','chore','task','feature','epic')` and `classify.py:52` raises on anything else, so filing a docs bead and running `loop advance --work-type docs` is a hard failure. loop.py:76 narrows leaves further to bug/chore/task.

2. `worktree-isolation/skill.yaml:17` says merging a finished worktree branch back is 'not yet part of basicly worktree'. It is: `basicly worktree` exposes `merge` and `merge-queue`, and merge.py is the merge orchestrator.

3. `worktree-isolation/skill.yaml:46` and architecture.md:1045 both say `[worktree].concurrency` defaults to 4. `config.py:360` sets `DEFAULT_WORKTREE_CONCURRENCY = 5`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the tool-br skill when it lists work types then it distinguishes br types from the loop work types and says which value to classify a docs bead as
- Given the worktree-isolation skill when it describes the worktree lifecycle then it lists merge and merge-queue and makes no not-yet claim about them
- Given the documented worktree concurrency default when it is read then no document restates the number at all and the only statement of it is DEFAULT_WORKTREE_CONCURRENCY
- Given a top-level command that owns subcommands when docs-claims runs then every subcommand must appear in a section 8 row whose command cell names that parent and the check fails when one is removed
- Given the tool-br skill's work-type lists when docs-claims runs then they are asserted against WORK_TYPES and the loop leaf types rather than hand maintained

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/tool-br/skill.yaml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/worktree-isolation/skill.yaml`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

payload.title: A fresh install fails its own Codex skill listing budget

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-6c97zx` drew the loop as a serpentine of eight nodes: an `intake` hopper, six stations, and a `done` sink. The sink is placed with `_place(len(STATIONS))`, which is index 6 — `ship`. It belongs at index 7.

## Measured

```text
$ python -c "from basicly import board_diagram as d; ..."
  0 intake     (150.0, 66.0)
  6 ship       (430.0, 196.0)
  7 done       (150.0, 196.0)   <- where the sink belongs
sink drawn (430.0, 196.0)       <- what the code does
```

So the `done` terminal is drawn at `ship`'s centre. Terminals are painted before stations, so the station box covers it: on a rendered board the sink's dashed shape, its closed count and its name are invisible, and its detail line (`main · <head>`) appears under the `ship` box where it reads as `ship`'s.

## Why no gate caught it

`check_render_overflow.py` reports a pairwise intersection of the boxes **that carry text**, and these two do not intersect: the sink's count is centre-anchored at 430 while `ship`'s is start-anchored at 338, so the runs miss each other by a few units. The element is not clipped either — it is drawn, at full size, underneath something opaque.

`tests/test_board_diagram.py::test_every_placement_is_inside_the_drawing_surface` asserts no two *stations* share a centre. It does not compare the terminals against them.

payload.description:
## Context

The residual risk of the grant decision (basicly-hnnmk9.1, owner 2026-09-05), stated rather than argued away.

With `spend.halted` no longer gating anything (basicly-vrgi1jk), an unattended pass is bounded only by `--max-passes` and the 7200s runner timeout. `--max-passes 50` with nobody watching is unbounded in practice. That is the state `basicly-vz78` was filed for: *"an unbounded pass looked exactly like a checked one."*

## Why the grant was never that bound

Measured 2026-09-05. `basicly-fiow1sr` ran to **17,838,762** run-record tokens against a 7,934,065 forecast while `basicly loop session` reported `grant: L1, 0/10000000 tokens under this grant`. Grant spend accrues per **completed** run record, so a lane in flight contributes zero until it finishes.

Both admission sites confirm the shape - `supervise.py:1401` and `supervise.py:1971` test only whether a `token_budget` **exists**, never whether spend is under it:

```python
if admission.grant is not None and admission.grant.token_budget is not None:
    return None
```

So the ceiling is sampled at lane **boundaries**, and a lane is where the spend happens. That is why it appeared to do nothing until it killed something.

I stopped that lane by hand at 17.8M because the owner had authorised about 8M. The engine would not have.

## What this record is

The bound at the place spend happens: the runner watches its own lane and stops it at a stated ceiling, reporting the figure. Not a permission and not a gate on anyone else - one process, its own spend, its own limit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a lane passes its token ceiling, THE RUNNER SHALL stop that lane and record why, and SHALL refuse nothing else.
- THE CEILING SHALL be a runner setting, not a grant field, so exhausting it cannot revoke an autonomy level - the coupling basicly-hnnmk9.1 was filed against.
- WHERE no ceiling is set, THE RUNNER SHALL behave exactly as it does today.
- THE STOPPED LANE SHALL leave its worktree and its uncommitted work intact, because basicly-ncday7 showed that landing an unreviewed diff is worse than stopping.
- A TEST SHALL drive a lane past a small ceiling and assert it stopped, the figure was recorded and the worktree survived.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_runner*.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: dispatch with a 100k ceiling and read the lane stop with its worktree intact

A runner setting and never a grant field, which is the whole difference from the bound it replaces: the grant remainder is a session fact every sibling lane moves. Off by default. The live figure over-reports the run record by 1.67x to 3.04x, median 2.31, and runner_usage already states erring high is the safe direction for a ceiling.

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "status != \"closed\"" src/basicly/supervise.py
uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-vkh0
uv run python -c "
import json
for l in open('.beads/issues.jsonl'):
    l = l.strip()
    if l:
        d = json.loads(l)
        if d['id'] == 'basicly-vkh0.4':
            print(d['id'], d['status'])"
```

Observed - `preflight basicly-vkh0` reports `3 open child(ren)` and sizes `basicly-vkh0.4` into the band table, while the tracker records that bead as `deferred`. Expected - a bead someone explicitly deferred is not a candidate for funding or dispatch.

## Context

`SessionState.open_children` at `supervise.py:317-319` is `status != "closed"`. Beads has at least three non-closed statuses and `deferred` is one of them, so deferring a bead removes it from nothing: it stays in the candidate set, it is sized into the band table, it counts toward `children_open`, and it is included in the `cap x per-lane` forecast that decides whether a pass can be funded at all.

Concretely, `basicly-vkh0` has one genuinely ready child (`basicly-vkh0.10`, P0, in band at 26780), one child with no readable scope (`basicly-vkh0.9`, which therefore draws the 15245717 per-lane assumption), and `basicly-vkh0.4`, deferred since 2026-07-30. Preflight reports three, and the forecast it produces is large enough to escalate against the epic's remaining 8000000 grant - so **a deferred bead can block a pass that its ready siblings could afford**. That is the reverse of what deferring is for.

Two things worth separating. `deferred` should not be dispatchable, and that is this bead. Whether an *unsized* child should be allowed to draw the per-lane assumption into a funding decision is a different question and is closer to `basicly-jr0l.61` (start the lanes a short remainder funds instead of refusing the whole pass).

Also note `derive_phase`'s fan-in reads the same property: `all_children_closed` is `bool(self.children) and not self.open_children`, so an epic whose only remaining child is deferred can never reach done. That is the same root cause and must be fixed with it rather than separately - a deferred child should not hold an epic open forever.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an epic with a deferred child when a pass is preflighted then that child is not sized into the band table and does not contribute to the forecast
- Given an epic whose every non-deferred child is closed when it is advanced then the fan-in treats it as complete rather than waiting on the deferred child
- Given the set of beads statuses when the dispatch candidate rule is expressed then it names the statuses it admits rather than excluding only closed and a test covers a deferred child at both sites

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
payload.title: A deferred child is still dispatchable and still holds its epic open

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a person reads a story in the tracker, I want to see which epic it belongs to and which stories or epics it must wait on, as a dependency graph with the parent-child relations, so I can tell where the work sits and what unblocks it.

## Context

Owner request 2026-10-13, in their words: "for the tracker UI i need a dependency and parent-child views. I want to know to which epic a story belongs to, and i want to know on which story (or epic) it needs to wait. A dependency graph with child-parent relations. Do a research on how to do that and how to visualize. now you have the designer specialist that you can employ too."

The owner asked to do this together with the tracker and board design work (basicly-lc2bd3v.11, basicly-gdsboki.5), because the work is connected. Research and a designer proposal come first; the build follows the owner's choice.
payload.title: Show each record's epic path and what it waits on, with a dependency and parent-child graph in the tracker

payload.text: [design proposal 2026-10-29, designer agent, read-only] Recommended: Option A, an epic path line above the title plus a WAITS ON / UNBLOCKS block above Context, with a Show chain tree down to the blocker that can start now; then Option C, an epic map that lays out an epic's children in waves (topological over blocks, rank within a wave), no drawn lines, at #<redacted:posix-absolute-path><id>/map. Rejected: a three-column view (titles cut to 18 chars, stacks into A below 900 px) and a whole-ledger graph (largest component 845 of 1,810 records). Measured on this ledger: parent chains at most 3 deep, 2 records with two parents, at most 109 children, 0 cycles, 0 missing targets. API additions: issue_type and close_resolution on linked records and an ancestors list in record_view._edges; status on summary edges in queries._edges_of. Open questions for the owner: show what a story's epic waits on (rec: yes, muted, says it does not hold the story); show that an epic waits on its open children (rec: yes); map as a mode of the epic (rec: yes); compute ancestors on the server (rec: yes).

[owner decision 2026-10-29] Approved the recommended design: build Option A (epic path line plus WAITS ON / UNBLOCKS block with Show chain) first, then Option C (epic map as a mode of the epic at #<redacted:posix-absolute-path><id>/map). Show what a story's epic waits on as a muted line that says it does not hold the story; show that an epic waits on its open children; compute ancestors on the server. Planned for v0.34.

payload.description:
## Context

Second defect recorded on `basicly-jn1x`, **not fixed there** because its precondition is not met.

`runner.py` applies both flags on one argv: `_apply_role(spec, _apply_model(spec, ...), role)`.
Measured on the probe that filed `jn1x`: `--agent probeagent(model: haiku) --model sonnet` ran the
turn on **sonnet**, so `--model` overrides the model an agent definition declares.

The run record then reports `tier_honoured: true` for that shape, because the field means
something narrower than a reader assumes - `run_record.py` documents it as False "only when a tier
was asked for and the family could not pin one at all". A role whose declared tier was overridden
is not that case, so the record is not wrong by its own contract and is misleading against the
question a reader asks it.

## Why it is not actionable yet

Decision D30: a provider model id never appears in an agent file, generated or not. So **no
projected agent carries a `model:` today** and there is nothing for `--model` to override. The
injection that would put one there is `basicly-a3yi`, still open.

Filing a fixture for the override now would be inventing the shape rather than observing it, which
is the failure this repository has already paid for twice.

## What changed under it

`basicly-jn1x` landed the recorded argv, so the co-occurrence is now **visible in the ledger**: a
record whose command carries both `--agent` and `--model` is exactly the shape at risk. Before
that, 0 of 357 records named either flag and the question could not be asked of the data at all.

## When to take this

After `basicly-a3yi`. Then decide whether the fix is to drop `--model` when a role declares one,
or to widen `tier_honoured` to mean "the tier that was asked for is the tier that ran" - the
second is the honest reading of the name and changes an existing contract, so it is a decision
rather than a patch.
payload.title: a model pin silently overrides the model a role declares once tier injection lands

`runner.py` applies both flags on one argv: `_apply_role(spec, _apply_model(spec, ...), role)`.
Measured on the probe that filed `jn1x`: `--agent probeagent(model: haiku) --model sonnet` ran the
turn on **sonnet**, so `--model` overrides the model an agent definition declares.

The run record then reports `tier_honoured: true` for that shape, because the field means
something narrower than a reader assumes - `run_record.py` documents it as False "only when a tier
was asked for and the family could not pin one at all". A role whose declared tier was overridden
is not that case, so the record is not wrong by its own contract and is misleading against the
question a reader asks it.

## Why it is not actionable yet

Decision D30: a provider model id never appears in an agent file, generated or not. So **no
projected agent carries a `model:` today** and there is nothing for `--model` to override. The
injection that would put one there is `basicly-a3yi`, still open.

Filing a fixture for the override now would be inventing the shape rather than observing it, which
is the failure this repository has already paid for twice.

## What changed under it

`basicly-jn1x` landed the recorded argv, so the co-occurrence is now **visible in the ledger**: a
record whose command carries both `--agent` and `--model` is exactly the shape at risk. Before
that, 0 of 357 records named either flag and the question could not be asked of the data at all.

## When to take this

After `basicly-a3yi`. Then decide whether the fix is to drop `--model` when a role declares one,
or to widen `tier_honoured` to mean "the tier that was asked for is the tier that ran" - the
second is the honest reading of the name and changes an existing contract, so it is a decision
rather than a patch.

## Steps to Reproduce

The override itself reproduces today; the *projected-agent* shape does not, and step 1 is
the control that says which.

1. Establish the precondition, so nobody mistakes a green result here for a fixed defect:

       rg -n '^model:' .claude/agents/*.md .github/agents/*.agent.md
       rg -n '^tools:' .claude/agents/*.md .github/agents/*.agent.md

   Observed 2026-08-19: the first command returns nothing. **The second is its positive
   control** - same pattern shape, same files - and returns a `tools:` line for every one of
   the projected agents. So no projected agent carries a `model:` today (decision D30), and
   the injection that would put one there, `basicly-a3yi`, is still **open**. There is
   nothing for `--model` to override on the projected path yet.
2. Reproduce the override on a hand-authored agent, which is the shape this record's
   measurement came from: define a probe agent declaring `model: haiku` in its own
   frontmatter, then run one turn passing both flags on the same argv -
   `--agent probeagent --model sonnet`.
3. Read which model actually served the turn.
4. Read the argv assembly that produces the collision, and the field that reports on it:

       rg -n '_apply_role\(spec, _apply_model' src/basicly/runner.py
       rg -n 'tier_honoured' src/basicly/run_record.py

Observed - this record's measurement, on the probe that filed `basicly-jn1x`: the turn ran on
**sonnet**, so `--model` overrode the model the agent definition declared. Re-checked
2026-08-19, `runner.py` still composes both flags on one argv as
`_apply_role(spec, _apply_model(spec, _apply_sandbox(spec, argv)), role)`, so the ordering
that produces the override is unchanged. The run record then reports `tier_honoured: true`
for that shape, because the field means only "a tier was asked for and the family could not
pin one at all" - which this is not.

Expected: a role that declares a model is not silently overridden by `--model`; either the
flag is dropped when a role declares one, or `tier_honoured` means "the tier that was asked
for is the tier that ran" and reports False here. The second changes an existing contract,
so it is a decision rather than a patch.

**Ordering.** Take this after `basicly-a3yi`. Until then step 1 has no projected `model:` to
find, and a test fixture asserting the projected shape would be invented rather than
observed.

payload.text:
UNBLOCKED 2026-09-16. This record's precondition was "once tier injection lands". It has landed on claude - status.yaml now grades `Tier injection on claude` as shipped, proven on three spawn paths.

The shape this record names is live in the recorded history. A dispatch argv reads `["claude", "--agent", "implementer", "--model", "claude-opus-5", "-p", ...]`, so `--agent` and `--model` are both applied by `_apply_role(spec, _apply_model(spec, ...), role)` and the pin wins.

It does not currently produce a wrong model, because the runner resolves the tier itself and the pin agrees with it - that run recorded `model_source: family default tier` and `tier_honoured: true`, and `implementer` is tier high, which resolves to `claude-opus-5`. **What stands is the reporting defect this record already names**: if the two ever disagree, the pin wins silently and `tier_honoured` still reports true, because the field means something narrower than a reader assumes.

Note the two paths are separate and only one is covered. The hook rewrites an **Agent tool** spawn, which is the in-session subagent path. `--agent`/`--model` is the **headless runner** path. Tier injection landing does not touch the second, so this record is now the only thing standing between a declared tier and the dispatch path the supervisor uses.

FIXED 2026-09-16, commit dec851c2.

**The fix is the first of the two options this record named, not the second.** It asked whether to drop `--model` when a role declares one, or to widen `tier_honoured` to mean "the tier asked for is the tier that ran". Neither was needed once the real cause was seen: `--model` was not overriding the role's tier, it was carrying the **pass default** because nothing ever consulted the role.

`resolve_model` took `spec.tier`, which is the configured `runner.default_tier`, and never looked at the role named on the same argv. `runner.role_tier(repo_root, role)` now reads the role's declared tier from the catalog and it outranks the pass default. Precedence is: an explicit `spec.model` pin, then the role's own tier, then the family default.

Measured against a pass default of `high`:

    role=tester     tier=low      source=role tier            model=claude-haiku-4-5
    role=validator  tier=medium   source=role tier            model=claude-sonnet-5
    role=reviewer   tier=high     source=role tier            model=claude-opus-5
    role=architect  tier=maximum  source=role tier            model=claude-fable-5-1
    role=None       tier=high     source=family default tier  model=claude-opus-5

**The reporting defect dissolves rather than being redefined.** `--model` is set from the resolution, so the pin and the declared tier are now the same value and `tier_honoured` answers the question a reader actually asks. No contract was widened.

Three tests pin it in `tests/test_config.py`: the role beats the pass default, no role still falls back, and a role the catalog does not declare falls back rather than raising. `lint-imports` confirms `runner` may read `agents` - it sits above it in the declared layers.

**Both spawn paths are now covered.** The `PreToolUse` hook covers an in-session Agent-tool spawn; this covers the headless runner path the supervisor uses.

payload.description:
## Context

Found by the lane-C survey 2026-08-14. The most expensive class here, and this repository has paid for it twice already.

Which routes an escalation offers is composed as free prose in five wordings, at `policy.py:638-640`, `supervise.py:2730`, `:3709`, `:3717` and `:3842`. It is then re-derived by parsing on the consumer side.

```text
cli.py:3608   _OFFERS_PARK = "or park?"        suffix match
cli.py:3576   _RETRY_ANSWER                    leading-token regular expression
policy.py     gate_from_rework_escalation      question-regex gate extraction
policy.py     gate_from_unreliable_escalation  applied at cli.py:3672
```

## Two shipped defects of exactly this shape are already on record

The docstrings themselves record them at `cli.py:3585-3587` and `cli.py:3627-3631`. `basicly-4tjt` offered three routes and implemented none. `basicly-vkjt` offered a park route whose answer silently did nothing.

## The second half

The consequence carriers `_carry_out_rework_retry`, `_carry_out_rework_hold` and `_announce_land_anyway` are at `cli.py:3582-3680`. They are engine semantics that live in the command-line tier, reachable and tested only through the argument parser. That is the shape `basicly-tcmy.16` names for the install lifecycle.

Today the three answer sites stay consistent only because the engine sites self-answer with a marker the carriers happen to refuse.

## Acceptance

- When an escalation is enqueued, then the decision item carries structured route and gate fields written by its composer.
- When an answer is recorded, then the consequence is selected on those fields, from a module below the command-line tier.
- When the suffix and regular-expression parsers are searched, then none remains.
- When a new escalation wording is added, then its routes cannot detach from their consequences.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/landing_gate.py`
- `src/basicly/working_set.py`
- their tests

## Depends on

Serialize with `basicly-tcmy.12`, which touches the same region of the command-line module.

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_cli_policy.py -q`, then answer a real escalation on a fixture session and read the recorded consequence.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a bead whose ## Scope heading yields no parseable glob when basicly policy dor runs on it then it reports the heading parsed to nothing as a visible warning without changing the ready verdict and basicly policy scaffold emits a ## Scope section in the backticked-glob form
payload.description:
## Problem

Guidance tells an author to give a bead a `## Scope` section so its lane can be sized, and
that is not sufficient: `decompose.parse_scope_section` only collects lines matching
`_SCOPE_LINE`, which requires a **backticked glob**. A section whose entries are bare
paths, or paths with a trailing parenthetical note, parses to an empty tuple - so the bead
is indistinguishable from one that declared no scope at all.

The failure is silent and it points the wrong way: the author sees a `## Scope` heading in
the bead and believes the lane is sized, while every gate that consumes the scope treats it
as undeclared. `basicly-jr0l.60` shipped the fix that makes an undeclared scope *visible*
at the band gate, which is what exposed how common this is.

Measured on this repo's own tracker, 2026-08-01, with `supervise.admit_working_set`:

```
basicly-jr0l.35  undeclared      basicly-jr0l.44  undeclared
basicly-jr0l.43  undeclared      basicly-jr0l.45  undeclared
basicly-jr0l.53  undeclared      basicly-jr0l.60  undeclared
basicly-jr0l.24  CHECKED, 123139 working-set tokens
```

`basicly-jr0l.60` carries a `## Scope` heading listing three real files and still sizes to
nothing, because its entries read `- src/basicly/supervise.py  (admit_working_set ...)`.
`basicly-jr0l.24` is the only one that parsed, and the only one whose entries are
backticked. So the one bead the band gate has ever refused is also the only bead that was
ever eligible to be refused.

Consequences: an unsizeable lane is bounded at the conservative assumed figure
(16002352 tokens), which makes a five-lane forecast ~80M and a 21M grant fund one lane;
and `jr0l.44`'s landing scope check is inert on the same beads, because it reads the same
parser.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. File a bead whose description contains a `## Scope` section with a bare path entry,
   for example `- src/basicly/loop.py`.
2. Run `python -c "from pathlib import Path; from basicly import decompose;
   print(decompose.resolve_dispatch_sizing(Path('.'), '<bead>'))"`.

Observed: `SizingLookup(sizing=None, absence='undeclared')`. Expected: either a real
sizing, or a warning at authoring time that the section parsed to nothing.

## Suggested Direction

Two halves, and the first matters more:

- **Say it where beads are authored.** `basicly policy scaffold` emits the DoR headings, so
  it should emit a `## Scope` example in the parseable form. The `harness-loop` skill tells
  an author to declare a scope without saying what a scope line looks like.
- **Report a section that parsed to nothing.** A `## Scope` heading whose body yields zero
  globs is almost certainly an authoring error rather than a deliberate empty scope, and it
  is cheap to detect: heading present, entries absent. `basicly policy dor` or
  `catalog lint` could say so. Fail-closed on it would block most of the tracker, which is
  the objection that settled basicly-vz78, so this should warn and be visible - not refuse.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
- `.claude/skills/harness-loop/SKILL.md`
- `.agents/skills/harness-loop/SKILL.md`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
- `tests/test_cli_policy.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Found while landing two lanes on 2026-08-14.

Each ratchet gate ratchets its own waiver count. Nothing counts them together, and nothing reviews one after it is granted.

```text
module-size waivers      1 -> 2   basicly-r343, bought on cost, expires under basicly-kr7t
comment-density waivers  1 -> 2   basicly-feje, bought on cohesion, no expiry needed
```

Two waivers in one session, from two lanes that were not about size. Both were argued honestly and both are defensible on their own. The pattern is the finding, not either grant.

## Why a per-gate count is not enough

A waiver is the one escape every size rule leaves open, so it is where pressure goes when a ratchet blocks unrelated work. The `basicly-r343` case is the shape to watch: the ratchet refused **any** change to a file, so the fix could not land without either a waiver or a refactor that had nothing to do with the bug.

The design already says waivers are ratcheted so the count may not grow silently. It grows visibly and nobody reads the number, because it is a parenthetical inside one gate's pass line.

## The distinction that must survive

Not every waiver is debt. Two kinds exist and they need different handling.

- **Bought on cohesion.** A genuinely small module whose prose is the contract it carries. Correct, permanent, and no follow-up is owed. `lens_review.py` is this.
- **Bought on cost.** The ratchet refused a change and the real fix was out of scope. Debt, and it must expire. `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` is this, and `basicly-kr7t` retires it.

Today the record cannot tell them apart. A reader sees a count.

## Acceptance

- When any waiver is granted, then its record states which of the two kinds it is.
- When a waiver is bought on cost, then it names the bead that retires it, and a check fails once that bead closes and the waiver remains.
- When the gates report, then one line states the total waiver count across all gates and how many are debt.
- Given today's four waivers, when the check runs, then it reports two cohesion and two cost, and it does not fail.

## Scope

- `.scripts/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `basicly.d/`
- `tests/`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly verify --mode fast` prints one waiver total with its split, and a fixture whose retiring bead is closed while its waiver stands fails the check.

payload.description:
## Context

The owner read the board and reported *"there is one failing pytest"*. The tree was green: `uv run pytest -q` gave 5262 passed, and `pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25` — the gate's own invocation — gave 5262 passed. The verdict on the page was **46 minutes old** and predated four merges.

The board invited the reading. Measured on the served document:

```text
snapshot generated_at : 2026-09-05T14:07:00Z
gates.recorded_at     : 2026-09-05T13:20:36Z   -> 46 minutes older
```

and the header drew both facts adjacent:

```text
gates 1 FAILING: pytest · mode full · recorded 2026-09-05T13:20:36Z
...                                                as of 5s ago
```

`as of 5s ago` is the *snapshot's* age. The gate verdict is a **bare absolute stamp** beside it, on a page whose vocabulary is otherwise ages throughout — `as of 5s ago`, `13 DAYS`, `since Sat 22 Aug 19:51 UTC`, `stale after 60s`. A reader has to notice that one figure is a different kind from every other and subtract by hand.

## This is the false-calm defect inverted

`basicly-2no50w` fixed the board saying nothing was waiting when something was. This is the board saying the tree is broken when it is not, and it costs the same thing: the reader stops trusting the region. `board_serve`'s own docstring states the principle — *"The board is as fresh as the producer that wrote its snapshot, and it always shows how old that snapshot is"* — and the `gates` section has a second, older freshness the page never states as an age.

## Why the stamp cannot just be reformatted

Two figures, two meanings. The snapshot age says how old the *document* is; the gate age says how old the *verdict* is, and the second can be arbitrarily older because it comes off `.basicly/usage/verify-run.json`, written whenever someone last ran `basicly verify`. A wall that has been up all day can be five seconds fresh and carry a verdict from breakfast.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the gate verdict is drawn, ITS AGE SHALL be stated in the same coarse unit the page uses elsewhere, not as an absolute stamp alone.
- WHEN the verdict is older than the document by more than the freshness window, THE REGION SHALL mark it stale, and a failing verdict older than that SHALL NOT be drawn in the alarm register.
- WHERE no verdict has been recorded at all, THE REGION SHALL say so rather than reading green.
- WHEN the age is drawn, IT SHALL come from the document's own `generated_at` and not from the reader's clock, so two viewers of one snapshot agree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Serve the board with a verify artifact an hour old and read the gates cell; then record a fresh pass and read it again.

Age is a proxy and the record says so: the real discriminator is the head the verdict was taken at, which the artifact does not record - filed as basicly-1y9hb5. [session handover 2026-09-13] Design session, no engine code changed. Architecture and backlog only.

STATE: main clean at 48e17e5f, level with origin. `uv run pytest -q` 5772 passed 1 xfailed. `basicly verify --mode full` All checks passed.

WHAT LANDED. Architecture section 31A "The software factory" (end of Part IV, no renumbering), section 32.11 "The two fields verification and validation test against", a new opening to 26.1, six decision records D-45 to D-50, one amended non-goal row, three glossary terms (seat, announcement, watermark) plus acceptance criteria and requirements pinned to their ISO clauses. Epic basicly-tyz08gd with 16 children, every one passing the definition of ready. Ten status.yaml rows.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED THE DESIGN. A warm resumed session costs 0.20x and 0.19x of a fresh one for the same task at the same token count (basicly-8724lqq, five live dispatches, 0.94 usd list). The saving is the avoided cache write, not fewer tokens. I argued the opposite first, in token counts, and was wrong. The corollary is the rule: a seat idle past its cache window re-writes a larger prefix at full price, so a seat is busy inside the window or the engine ends it, and the pull queue is what holds that.

TWO THINGS THE OWNER WAS RIGHT ABOUT AND I WAS NOT. Long-lived warm workers are cheaper, measured above. And validation needs a stored standard: the validator's contract names "the requirement that asked for it" five times and 0 of 1,347 records carry one. D-50 makes requirements and acceptance_criteria typed fields, required at the definition of ready on every work type.

OPEN, IN THE ORDER I WOULD TAKE THEM.
1. basicly-zq9i2m and basicly-884gj4 both block the factory epic by the owner's sequencing choice. One supervised pass landing clean, and the cost-per-landed-unit instrument, come before any factory work.
2. basicly-awawrt3 - a lane carries 9.3x the scope its plan declares and the working set is re-read 26x. Cost is working set times turns, so this is the largest single lever in the system and its cause is unknown.
3. basicly-vk97szk - the host will make bare mode the default for -p, and bare mode does not use the subscription login (verified live: apiKeySource none, exit 1). That is a dated cost regression with our name on it.
4. basicly-w921i6b - the cold arm of the warm-seat experiment. The release rule rests on an argument until it is priced.
5. basicly-xjd2 needs a human read, not an edge. Its own correction says its re-scope branch must be chosen deliberately; section 31A.7 just chose it, so the record is either closable or re-scopable to its surviving half.

LIMITS. The warm-seat result is two replications at two model turns per task, read-only tasks, every resume seconds after its predecessor. The ISO definitions came from secondary sources; iso.org returned 403. basicly-zk24ktw is a real fallback defect that reaches 2 of 294 records, not the live data.

[session handover 2026-09-16] Tier injection and the kits, not the factory. The factory epic below is untouched today; its own plan still stands.

STATE: main clean, level with origin after the push. `uv run basicly verify --mode full` PASS. `uv run pytest -q` 5791 passed 1 xfailed at the last full run.

SHIPPED. **Tier injection works on claude and is measured on three spawn paths**, not inferred: a `claude -p` dispatch here (validator, medium, ran sonnet), an in-session background subagent here (tester, low, ran haiku across all 7 of its assistant messages), and a `-p` spawn in a repository with no `.basicly/core` at all (scribe, low, ran haiku, 0.10 usd). status.yaml now grades `Tier injection on claude` as shipped and carries `Tier injection on copilot` as a separate building row.

FOUR DEFECTS FIXED, each found by running the thing as a consumer runs it.
1. The projector parsed `tier:` and never emitted it, so 0 of 11 projected agents carried one and the hook had nothing to read. It now writes into both agent roots and `tier` is reserved so a passthrough cannot shadow it.
2. `find_map` searched only `.basicly/core/models/`, which a standalone consumer has not got, so the vendored hook silently declined every rewrite. It now falls back to the map beside the kit, scoped to the project the kit sits inside.
3. `uninstall` deleted the kit and left the hook pointing at a dead path. `install_hook --uninstall` exists and `kit_installer` runs it before deleting anything.
4. The headless runner pinned `--model` from the pass default and never consulted the role, so a declared tier reached the Agent-tool path and not the runner path. `runner.role_tier` now outranks the pass default, which also dissolves basicly-trxy's reporting defect rather than redefining `tier_honoured`.

ALL THREE KITS VERIFIED BOTH WAYS. Standalone from a built wheel into a fresh `git init` directory: install, configure, work, uninstall with **no residue** measured across the kit tree, both skill roots, the tier hook and the tracker's own git lines. Through `basicly install` in a throwaway repo: the comments gate refused a real commit, the tracker read and wrote, the tier hook wired. `tests/test_kit_consumer_install.py` pins all of it, 10 tests, which closes what basicly-wjx0soa asked for.

DOCS. `docs/reference/kits.md` is new and documents every kit command with every flag, what each `init` writes and what `uninstall` takes back. Every command in it was executed before publishing; two apparent failures were my probe, not the docs. The README gained the tier wiring, what `init` configures, and a reference table that also links `cli.md`, which it had never linked.

RETRO APPLIED, NOT JUST FILED. `external-facts` carries three new clauses and basicly-xliyth9 is closed: a cost claim names its priced components; a person-reported disagreement against a vendor figure is settled by running the vendor path; a probe bounds what it proves and its confound is named. OPEN, IN THE ORDER I WOULD TAKE THEM.
1. basicly-a3yi and basicly-u2hl.41 - copilot. Deliberately left. That host reads no tier; it selects a subagent model in configuration. `~/.copilot/session-store.db` table `assistant_usage_events` reads the model per turn **for free**, and the test must use a tier whose model differs from the configured default or it is confounded, as mine was.

## Trigger

When a gate tests a change against its acceptance criteria, I want the criteria read from one store, so I can stop maintaining a field that 467 records carry and nothing tests against.

## Requirements

R1. One representation of the acceptance criteria is authoritative, and a reader cannot pick the weaker one by accident.
R2. A record written before the change still yields its criteria after it, with no criterion lost.
R3. A reader can tell a migrated record from an unmigrated one without guessing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a record carrying the `acceptance_criteria` field, then `acceptance` comes from the field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When a record carries only the legacy `## Acceptance Criteria` heading, then the migration writes the field and leaves the description prose untouched. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration has run over the whole ledger, then every record that held the heading holds the field, and the criterion count per record is unchanged. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration runs a second time, then it writes nothing and exits zero. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_plan_record.py tests/test_tracker_migrate.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture D-50. Measured 2026-09-13 over 1,347 created events: the field is on 467 records and the heading on 761. `plan_record.section_entries` reads the heading today and `tracker_write._say_criteria` reads the field only to print a closing reminder.

payload.value:
## Trigger

When a gate tests a change against its acceptance criteria, I want the criteria read from one store, so I can stop maintaining a field that 467 records carry and nothing tests against.

## Requirements

R1. One representation of the acceptance criteria is authoritative, and a reader cannot pick the weaker one by accident.
R2. An open record that was written before the change still yields its criteria after it, with no criterion lost.
R3. A closed record stays readable as evidence, and nothing rewrites a line of the log to achieve that.
R4. The second store cannot grow back after the switch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a record carrying the `acceptance_criteria` field, then `acceptance` comes from the field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a **closed** record carrying only the legacy heading, then the heading is read as a fallback. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for an **open** record carrying only the legacy heading, then the read is refused and the refusal names the missing field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When the migration runs, then it appends one update event per open record that holds the heading and not the field, and edits no line that already exists. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration has run, then every open record that held the heading alone holds the field, and the criterion count per record is unchanged. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration runs a second time, then it writes nothing and exits zero. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When a caller writes a `## Acceptance Criteria` heading on an open record after the switch, then the write is refused. [check: `tests/test_tracker_write.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_plan_record.py tests/test_tracker_migrate.py -q`

## Scope

The open set only. Measured 2026-09-13 over 9,427 events: 1,361 records, 341 open; 572 carry the heading alone and **150 of those are open**. The 1,020 closed records are not migrated - a closed record is evidence and will never be verified again.

The 202 records that carry both stores are **out of scope here**, because 94 of them disagree and a script that picks a winner loses content. That work is its own record.

## Design notes

Architecture section 32.11 and D-50, under the append-only rule section 32.8 already binds: a migration is a reader change plus a writer switch, with no edit to any line that exists. A rewrite of the log is refused by D-27, which makes `git diff` and `git blame` the whole audit trail.
